content: In certain carefully selected situations, specific strategies may be employed to expand access to treatment when the alternative is no treatment at all. For instance, ablation can be considered for a small, well-defined type 2 transformation zone, provided the probe tip can completely ablate the squamocolumnar junction epithelium. This requires the probe to reach the full extent, depth, and upper limit of the transformation zone. Additionally, adequate training for patient selection and follow-up must be available. Persistent, residual, or recurrent disease refers to the detection of histopathologically verified high-grade lesions, such as high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) or adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), at any time after initial treatment. Persistent or residual disease is identified when there is no documented absence of disease between the initial treatment and subsequent detection. Recurrent disease, on the other hand, is defined as the reappearance of high-grade lesions following a documented disease-free interval. Both conditions are considered treatment failures and may require retreatment. Studies often use terms like persistent/residual disease and recurrence interchangeably, but sub-analysis can help distinguish between them. The treatment of recurrent or persistent HSIL, CIN 2, or CIN 3 typically involves excision (e.g., large loop excision of the transformation zone [LLETZ] or cold knife conization [CKC]) or ablation, depending on eligibility and available techniques. AIS is treated with excision, while invasive cancers require more advanced interventions such as radical surgery or radiation therapy. The presence of disease should ideally be assessed beyond six months post-treatment, with a preferred follow-up period of 1–3 years. Recurrence may occur several years after treatment. The incidence of new high-grade lesions or cervical cancers (HSIL+ or CIN 2+) following treatment is defined as the detection of histopathologically confirmed cases, including HSIL, CIN 2/3, AIS, or invasive cancers. These cases are typically identified through active follow-up or linkage with screening registries. The cumulative rates of HSIL+ or CIN 2+ can be calculated per 100,000 person-years of observation. Treatment for high-grade lesions involves excision or ablation, while invasive cancers require radical surgery or radiation therapy. Mortality from cervical cancer is defined as deaths reported in the population following treatment within a defined time period. These deaths are assessed through linkage with cancer registries and mortality databases. Treatment coverage refers to the proportion of eligible women who complete treatment within a defined timeframe, typically 12 months. Low treatment coverage increases the risk of invasive cancer and reduces the effectiveness of screening programs. Treatment side effects and complications are categorized as either temporary side effects or more severe complications requiring intervention. Major infections, such as post-operative genital tract infections, may require antibiotics or hospitalization. Major bleeding, defined as post-operative bleeding requiring intervention, can lead to anemia, shock, or even death in severe cases. Pain associated with procedures is typically temporary and managed with analgesics. Cervical stenosis, or narrowing of the endocervical canal, may require dilation. Other complications include spontaneous abortions, premature rupture of membranes, preterm births, and perinatal deaths, each with specific consequences and management strategies. Infertility is defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Stigmatization, often associated with cervical cancer screening or treatment, can lead to social and psychological harm, including isolation, abuse, and altered health-seeking behavior. Increased viral shedding in women living with HIV may result in the transmission of the virus to uninfected partners. Acceptability of screening and treatment interventions is determined by the extent to which women, providers, or program managers consider the interventions appropriate based on their experiences and responses. This is a multifaceted construct influenced by cognitive and emotional factors.
